newsitem.title: USA: Final U.S. campaign debate offers Dole last chance.
newsitem.headline: Final U.S. campaign debate offers Dole last chance.

text.p: Republican Bob Dole may have his last chance to derail President Bill Clinton's seemingly unstoppable re-election drive when the two meet on Wednesday in their final campaign debate.

The 90-minute "town hall" style meeting in San Diego, California -- in which they will answer questions posed by undecided voters in the audience instead of by a moderator as in their first debate -- could be the last defining event of the campaign. Election Day is only three weeks away on Nov 5.
The big question is how aggressive Dole will be in going after the ethical record of Clinton's administration.

He has been hinting in recent days that he will get tough and his vice presidential running mate, Jack Kemp, seemed ready to take off the gloves despite having said last week that personal attacks were beneath Dole's dignity.

"It is clear that Travelgate and Filegate, the abuse of power, the arrogance of power, the possibility of a pardon (for Clinton's former Whitewater business partners) are not the type of things that we would want or expect from the Oval Office of the president of the United States," Kemp said in a campaign appearance.

"Travelgate" refers to the controversial firing of the White House travel office staff early in Clinton's term of office, which many regarded as an unwarranted exercise of personal power and favouritism.
"Filegate" is shorthand for the improper acquisition of hundreds of FBI files on Republicans by the White House personnel security office, also in 1993.

Clinton has also refused to rule out presidential pardons for some of his former partners in a failed Arkansas land investment. Several people have been convicted and some jailed on fraud and other charges stemming from separate incidents in the tangled financial controversy known as Whitewater.

With Clinton leading by a wide margin in public opinion polls, it is unclear whether an all-out attack by Dole would do much to change the race. It might even rebound against the Republican nominee, who has spent much of the campaign fighting against his own reputation for harshness.

"Time is running out for Dole and it is not surprising that he and his advisors have decided on the risky option of attacking Clinton's character. Nothing else has worked to date," said Reuters pollster John Zogby.
David Winston, a poll analyst for the Politics Now internet service, said the debate presented Dole with a faint last chance.
"Unless Dole surprises everyone in the next debate, it seems highly improbable that he can close this gap," he said.
Dole performed well in the first presidential debate on Oct. 6 in Hartford, Connecticut, and raised his favourability ratings by as much as 10 percentage points in some surveys.
But many voters still thought Clinton won the debate and the president emerged with his lead intact.
Dole himself seems torn about how far to go in attacking Clinton. In one interview last week, he said, "Whatever happens, I want to be at peace with myself when it's over."
As the final debate approached, he was getting plenty of advice from friends and allies about how to behave.

Some conservatives urged him to take the offensive. Others seemed resigned to the idea that the presidential election may already be lost and suggested Republicans should concentrate on keeping control of the Congress, which they won in 1994.

Much of the public certainly seems to think the election is over. Polls show almost three quarters of voters think Clinton will win and the viewing audience for the first debate, as well as last week's vice presidential debate, was down sharply from 1992 levels.
